tools.name: Claude Code
tools.what: Terminal coding agent from Anthropic
tools.verdict: The default harness in HN setup threads, often run through Desktop, Web or T3 Code. Praised for UX, skills and remote control; complaints are usage burn, ignored memory and unwanted files.

tools.name: Codex CLI
tools.what: OpenAI's terminal and desktop coding agent
tools.verdict: Usually the second subscription beside Claude, kept for review and second opinions. Credited with solid one-shots and fast-moving desktop features; dinged for hitting limits, bugs and loud default design taste.

tools.name: OpenCode
tools.what: Open-source terminal coding agent, any model
tools.verdict: The go-to open harness for DeepSeek, GLM or local models, often on the $10 OpenCode Go plan. Liked for per-agent model choice; a few moved on to Pi or T3 Code.

tools.name: Pi
tools.what: Minimal, hackable open-source coding agent harness
tools.verdict: A lean harness people bend to their own workflows, often with local or open models and the oh-my-pi fork. Liked for small prompts that fit tight context windows.

tools.name: DeepSeek Harness
tools.what: DeepSeek's own agent harness, desktop and TUI
tools.verdict: A cheap home setup for many commenters, paired with DeepSeek Flash for a few dollars a month. Praised for speed, value and plugins; web search is the recurring weak spot.

tools.name: Aider
tools.what: Open-source terminal pair programmer, manual context
tools.verdict: The pre-agent pair programmer, still liked by a few for manual file control and accuracy. Most commenters moved on, calling the manual context loading busywork next to agentic tools.

tools.name: Gemini CLI
tools.what: Google's open-source terminal agent for Gemini
tools.verdict: Older threads used it as the free option and liked its web search and code explanations. By late 2026 commenters call it deprecated for subscribers and replaced by Antigravity CLI.

tools.name: Copilot CLI
tools.what: GitHub Copilot's terminal coding agent
tools.verdict: Used where work already pays for GitHub Copilot; users say it runs close to Claude Code on the same models. Complaints target Autopilot mode, token burn and a thin plugin system.

tools.name: Goose
tools.what: Block's open-source extensible agent, Linux Foundation
tools.verdict: Block's open agent, now under the Linux Foundation, used for everyday tasks and custom bots. A few like its TUI; others found it too agentic or no better than prompting directly.

tools.name: Mistral Vibe
tools.what: Mistral's open-source terminal coding agent
tools.verdict: Mostly used as a cheap way to run hosted GLM-5.3. Fans call it fast and good enough; critics say the harness is sluggish, times out or ignores instructions.

tools.name: Muse Code
tools.what: Meta's terminal agent for Muse models
tools.verdict: Usually a cheap extra subscription next to Claude or Codex. One user relies on it for code review; others note tight limits on the top model or say they barely touch it.

tools.name: Kimi CLI
tools.what: Moonshot's open-source terminal agent for Kimi
tools.verdict: Moonshot's harness for Kimi models, used by Kimi subscribers. Commenters credit its checkpoint rollback for taming Kimi's tool-call loops; one critic called it a copy of basic harnesses.

tools.name: Qwen Code
tools.what: Alibaba's terminal agent for Qwen models
tools.verdict: Mostly paired with local Qwen models on home hardware. One user built a 3D game with it in two days; others found local runs slow and error-prone next to Claude Code.

tools.name: VS Code + Copilot
tools.what: GitHub Copilot agent inside VS Code
tools.verdict: Mostly the option work pays for. Praised for PR reviews, model choice and keep/undo diffs; others call it meh and dry next to Claude.

tools.name: Cursor
tools.what: AI-first VS Code fork with agents
tools.verdict: Often described as where commenters used to be. Usage limits and API-priced bills keep pushing people to a Claude subscription; a few still like its bundled plans.

tools.name: Zed
tools.what: Fast Rust editor with ACP agent support
tools.verdict: The editor many keep beside their agents, driving Claude or Codex over ACP or just reviewing code. Liked for speed and agent support; some found it overhyped or unusable without a GPU.

tools.name: Antigravity
tools.what: Google's agent IDE and CLI for Gemini
tools.verdict: The only subscription route to Gemini. Some use it daily for search and planning; complaints center on billing and account friction and a weak harness.

tools.name: Windsurf
tools.what: AI VS Code fork, team now at Google
tools.verdict: Mostly mentioned in the past tense now that its team went to Google. Older threads liked its codebase Q&A, autocomplete and parallel flows, but said it struggled on large files.

tools.name: Cline
tools.what: Open-source agent extension for VS Code
tools.verdict: Popular for pairing cheap API models like DeepSeek Flash, or local Ollama models, with VS Code. Liked for permission prompts and provider choice; several left after finding it slow and unstable.

tools.name: Kiro
tools.what: Amazon's spec-driven agentic VS Code fork
tools.verdict: Mostly a work-mandated tool at AWS shops. Its spec-driven workflow gets borrowed elsewhere; Amazon engineers say the harness trails Claude Code and degrades over long context.

tools.name: Roo Code
tools.what: Cline fork for VS Code, now discontinued
tools.verdict: Ran on your own API key or local models inside VS Code. Users liked its control, visible costs and architect and orchestrator modes; it has been discontinued, with forks carrying on.

tools.name: Kilo Code
tools.what: Roo Code fork for VS Code, JetBrains
tools.verdict: Run on your own keys or Kilo credits across many models. Users say it gets the job done; gripes are weak compaction and a recent version that feels blander.

tools.name: Neovim (CodeCompanion / avante)
tools.what: AI chat and edit plugins for Neovim
tools.verdict: Neovim users reach for CodeCompanion for in-editor chat and quick edits, handing bigger tasks to OpenCode or Claude Code. Local-model setups can loop, and completion trails Cursor Tab.

tools.name: JetBrains Junie
tools.what: JetBrains' coding agent inside its IDEs
tools.verdict: Popular with IntelliJ users, often paired with cheap Gemini Flash. Good for small, well-defined tasks and tests; quotas are tight and some rate the harness below Claude Code.

tools.name: Emacs gptel
tools.what: LLM client and agent toolkit for Emacs
tools.verdict: Built for human-in-the-loop work: chat, code review and questions inside Emacs. Praised for staying out of the way and tiny token bills; agentic features are mostly do-it-yourself.

tools.name: Continue
tools.what: Open-source assistant for VS Code and JetBrains
tools.verdict: Was the usual way to plug Ollama or LM Studio models into VS Code. Commenters report it was acquired by Cursor in 2026, and recent mentions are mostly about its future.

tools.name: Herdr
tools.what: Terminal workspace for many agent sessions
tools.verdict: Runs several Claude Code, Codex or Pi sessions side by side. Loved for agent-done pings and a pane overview; a few never clicked with it or switched to Rex.

tools.name: tmux + git worktrees
tools.what: DIY parallel agents with tmux, worktrees
tools.verdict: The do-it-yourself baseline: a worktree per task, a tmux pane per agent, send-keys for messages. Fans say the new agent IDEs only repackage it; many build their own wrappers on top.

tools.name: Paseo
tools.what: Open-source desktop and mobile agent interface
tools.verdict: A front end for Pi, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode agents. Liked for its phone app and client-server setup; reports of memory strain and hung sub-agent status updates.

tools.name: Gas Town
tools.what: Steve Yegge's multi-agent coding orchestrator
tools.verdict: Steve Yegge's many-agent orchestrator. On HN it is mostly a punchline: too complex, too opinionated and a token sink, with nobody showing evals against a plain harness.

tools.name: T3 Code
tools.what: Open-source GUI driving multiple agent harnesses
tools.verdict: Drives Claude Code, Codex and Pi from one UI across machines. Fans praise mid-conversation agent handoff and remote sessions; others found it buggy or heavy on resources.

tools.name: Beads
tools.what: Git-backed issue tracker for coding agents
tools.verdict: Gives agents epics, tasks and dependencies to pull from, and some teams run their whole backlog on it. Critics call it bloated and question why it needs a daemon and database.

tools.name: Orca
tools.what: Open-source agent IDE for worktrees, remote
tools.verdict: Often self-hosted, with a mobile app for steering agents away from the desk. Praised for remote SSH and multi-worktree views; one user hit install trouble on a headless server.

tools.name: Conductor
tools.what: Mac app for parallel worktree agents, closing
tools.verdict: Ran Claude and Codex in parallel git worktrees, and recent threads say it is winding down. Users liked it for mid-size tasks and review; gripes were weak multi-repo support and Mac-only builds.

tools.name: Juggler
tools.what: GUI coding agent from JUCE's creator
tools.verdict: Treats local and remote sessions the same, which suits cross-platform work. Users like the control and visibility; one found its nested output stressful, another wished it were less vibecoded.

tools.name: Ralph loop
tools.what: Loop-until-done agent prompting pattern
tools.verdict: A pattern, not a product: rerun the agent until the task list says done. Used for overnight PR polishing and test coverage; skeptics call it token burning that hides broken tests.

tools.name: Vibe Kanban
tools.what: Kanban board that dispatches coding agents
tools.verdict: Users liked managing agents across projects from one board, but its developers stopped investing in it, and some felt it added little to their productivity.

tools.name: Omnara
tools.what: Remote and API layer for coding agents
tools.verdict: Began as phone and web remote control for Claude Code and Codex, now pitched as a self-hostable agent API. One user relies on it in transit; another found alternatives more reliable.

tools.name: Sculptor
tools.what: Imbue's desktop UI for Claude Code
tools.verdict: A desktop UI for running Claude Code agents. The scraped comments are almost all about actual sculptors, so there are no recent user reports to summarize.

tools.name: Claude Code review
tools.what: Anthropic's managed PR review for Claude Code
tools.verdict: Used as a PR pass alongside Codex or as a local /review skill. The recurring complaint is price, quoted at $15 to $25 per review, plus slowness and reviews that need re-checking.

tools.name: Copilot code review
tools.what: GitHub's built-in AI pull request reviewer
tools.verdict: The low-friction pick for teams already on GitHub; several call its PR comments surprisingly insightful. Complaints center on noisy, overeager comments and the 2026 change billing reviews against Actions minutes.

tools.name: CodeRabbit
tools.what: AI pull request review bot
tools.verdict: The name people reach for when describing an AI PR reviewer, usually as the reference point. Few first-hand endorsements here; several teams say they had gripes or built their own instead.

tools.name: Cursor Bugbot
tools.what: Cursor's AI bug-finding PR reviewer
tools.verdict: The most praised review bot in these threads; users say it finds subtle bugs Claude and Codex miss. Downsides: inconsistent across rounds, and a move to per-run pricing drove some away.

tools.name: Codex code review
tools.what: OpenAI Codex reviewing PRs and diffs
tools.verdict: Popular as the cross-vendor second opinion: write with Claude, review with Codex. Praised for catching real bugs; criticized for endless nitpick loops and an opaque separate quota.

tools.name: Codex Security
tools.what: OpenAI's open-source security review CLI
tools.verdict: OpenAI's open-source security scanning CLI. The launch thread, answered by the Promptfoo team, is dominated by model refusals on defensive security work and slow access for open-source maintainers.

tools.name: Qodo
tools.what: AI code review and PR agent
tools.verdict: An AI PR reviewer that teams try and often drop over noise. One user likes it for speeding up human review rather than replacing it, and Bugbot gives more quota per dollar.

tools.name: Graphite
tools.what: Stacked PR tool with AI code review
tools.verdict: Mostly known for stacked PRs, with an AI review agent on top, and now part of Cursor. The one real user here credits stacks with keeping AI-era PRs small.

tools.name: Greptile
tools.what: Codebase-aware AI pull request reviewer
tools.verdict: A PR review bot that shows up in several stacks next to Codex and Claude Code. One user found few false positives; others found it noisy or pricey like its rivals.

tools.name: Open Code Review (Alibaba)
tools.what: Alibaba's open-source CLI code review tool
tools.verdict: Alibaba's open-sourced internal code review CLI. Commenters see the value in its curated rule files, which originally shipped in Chinese and prompted community translations; first-hand usage reports are scarce.

tools.name: Sourcery
tools.what: AI code review bot for PRs
tools.verdict: A PR review bot recommended alongside CodeRabbit for catching contract violations and antipatterns. Most support comes from one repeat commenter; a team user calls it chatty but improving.

tools.name: Sphinx
tools.what: Hook that quizzes you on AI code
tools.verdict: A Show HN hook that quizzes you on your AI's code before you ship it. The launch drew 253 points, but no user comments about it turned up.

tools.name: AGENTS.md
tools.what: Open instruction file format for coding agents
tools.verdict: The default home for project rules; nearly every setup described here has one, sometimes as CLAUDE.md. Pain points are files that keep growing and instructions agents still ignore.

tools.name: Agent Skills
tools.what: Open format for reusable agent instruction packs
tools.verdict: Widely used for project-specific workflows and teaching agents in-house tools. A vocal minority says too many skills pollute context and that stronger models increasingly do fine without them.

tools.name: Superpowers
tools.what: Skills library for structured Claude Code workflows
tools.verdict: A Claude Code skills pack that walks the agent through brainstorm, design doc, plan, then build. Fans like the structure; skeptics say current models do fine run raw.

tools.name: Spec Kit
tools.what: GitHub's spec-driven development toolkit
tools.verdict: GitHub's spec-driven development kit, used to force requirements, plan and tasks before code. The main complaint is volume: reams of repetitive markdown that are tedious to review.

tools.name: Context7
tools.what: MCP server for up-to-date library docs
tools.verdict: One of the standard MCP servers people install, used to pull current library docs so the agent stops guessing APIs. No complaints turned up in these threads.

tools.name: GitHub MCP server
tools.what: Official MCP server for GitHub APIs
tools.verdict: Used to let agents read issues, search dependency code and open PRs, even from ChatGPT. The open questions are whether it beats the gh CLI and how it ties into Copilot billing.

tools.name: Semble
tools.what: Token-efficient code search for agents
tools.verdict: A code search tool for agents that claims far fewer tokens than grep. Two users keep it beside ripgrep and Serena; a skeptic says models aren't trained to use such tools.

tools.name: rtk
tools.what: CLI proxy that compresses agent command output
tools.verdict: A shell wrapper that trims command output before it reaches the agent's context. Its own stats claim big savings, but independent benchmarks found agents take more turns and save little.

tools.name: Impeccable
tools.what: Design skill to de-slop AI frontends
tools.verdict: A design skill for stripping the generic AI look from frontends. Users say it removes slop tells more aggressively than rivals, though output is a starting point and token use is high.

tools.name: Graphify
tools.what: Codebase knowledge graph for coding agents
tools.verdict: Maps a codebase into a knowledge graph so agents spend fewer tokens. Mostly cited as the baseline rivals claim to beat; one tester found models can't use its output well.

tools.name: Figma MCP
tools.what: Figma's MCP server for design-to-code
tools.verdict: Turns Figma designs into code; two users credit it with faster, pixel-accurate page builds. Recent threads call it close to unusable and fault Figma for gating access to approved clients.

tools.name: Serena
tools.what: MCP server exposing LSP code tools
tools.verdict: An MCP server that gives agents language-server tools for symbol lookup, indexing and refactors. The few real users say it works well, including inside OpenCode and JetBrains IDEs.

tools.name: context-mode
tools.what: Plugin that shrinks MCP output in context
tools.verdict: A plugin that shrinks bulky MCP tool output before it hits the agent's context window. Only three real mentions, each from someone who keeps it in their standard setup.

tools.name: Playwright MCP
tools.what: Microsoft's MCP server for browser automation
tools.verdict: The default way to give an agent a browser, used daily for UI checks and scraping. Works out of the box; the complaints are slowness and heavy context use.

tools.name: Chrome DevTools MCP
tools.what: Official MCP server for Chrome DevTools
tools.verdict: Chosen over Playwright when the agent needs real DevTools: network requests, performance traces, Lighthouse audits. Users run it for automated QA and debugging; one says it clutters context.

tools.name: agent-browser
tools.what: Vercel's browser automation CLI for agents
tools.verdict: Vercel's browser automation CLI for coding agents, often benchmarked against Playwright MCP. Users say it works fine, and its bundled skill turns up issues they would not think to test.

tools.name: Firecrawl
tools.what: Web scraping and search API for LLMs
tools.verdict: A common scraping and search API for agents, rated well and self-hostable. Critics cite request logging, a skill that nudges agents to send feedback, and site owners paying for its customers' traffic.

tools.name: Lightpanda
tools.what: Lightweight headless browser written in Zig
tools.verdict: A Zig headless browser built for agents and scraping. One team got big CPU and memory wins over Chrome; others hit pages it can't render and note it's easy to detect.

tools.name: Stagehand
tools.what: AI browser automation framework by Browserbase
tools.verdict: Browserbase's open-source AI browser automation framework, with act, extract and observe calls and a cached replay layer. Threads are mostly vendor posts; one skeptic asks why not let agents write Playwright directly.

tools.name: Claude in Chrome
tools.what: Anthropic's Chrome extension browsing agent
tools.verdict: Used for web chores in your logged-in browser: pulling Strava GPX files, downloading Datadog logs, driving ChatGPT, validating UX. Weak spots include missed obvious errors, multi-account setups and click-hijack vulnerabilities.

tools.name: Vibium
tools.what: Browser automation for agents from Selenium's creator
tools.verdict: Browser automation for agents from Selenium's creator, with a CLI and agent skill. Most mentions come from the creator or people watching its Claude-coauthored repo; one user wants it leaner on tokens.

tools.name: browser-use
tools.what: Open-source framework for LLM web agents
tools.verdict: An open-source framework for LLM-driven web agents from YC W25, with 120k GitHub stars. Recent HN threads barely discuss it directly; it mostly appears as a benchmark comparison target.

tools.name: Scrapling
tools.what: Stealthy Python web scraping library
tools.verdict: A stealthy Python scraping library that agents call for fetching pages, often behind an MCP. One frequent user says it loads nearly any site, even Google results, though output can be context-heavy.

tools.name: Browser MCP
tools.what: MCP server that drives your browser
tools.verdict: Lets Cursor, Claude or VS Code drive your own browser. The Show HN drew 616 points, but later comments use 'browser MCP' generically, so there's little signal on this tool itself.

tools.name: Jina Reader
tools.what: URL-to-markdown API for LLMs
tools.verdict: An API that turns any URL into clean markdown for LLMs. Used as a first-pass fetcher that cuts page tokens sharply; the limit is it's read-only, with no clicking or form filling.

tools.name: Browserbase
tools.what: Hosted headless browser infrastructure for agents
tools.verdict: Hosted browsers for agents, from the company behind Stagehand. One startup builds on it for session persistence; site operators blame it and its peers for abusive bot traffic and captcha bypass.

tools.name: bubblewrap
tools.what: Linux namespace sandbox for agent processes
tools.verdict: The DIY pick on Linux: people wrap Claude Code, Codex and Pi in bwrap scripts the harness cannot disable. Main knock: Linux only, and weaker than a microVM.

tools.name: Docker Sandboxes
tools.what: MicroVM sandboxes for running coding agents
tools.verdict: Where people run Claude Code and Codex in yolo mode, inside a microVM rather than a container. Praised for solid isolation; knocked for workflow friction and closed source.

tools.name: OpenShell
tools.what: NVIDIA policy-controlled runtime for agent fleets
tools.verdict: NVIDIA's policy layer for agent fleets, used by some teams to run Claude Code under granular permissions. Sceptics call it overcomplicated next to bwrap or plain Docker.

tools.name: Apple container
tools.what: Apple's lightweight Linux VM containers for macOS
tools.verdict: Mac users build agent sandboxes on it because each container is a lightweight Linux VM. Still called a work in progress, needs macOS 26, and you must block network access yourself.

tools.name: Dev containers
tools.what: Open spec for containerised development environments
tools.verdict: The no-new-tool answer: run the agent inside the devcontainer you already have. Protects against agent stupidity, not malice, and locking down the network takes real customisation.

tools.name: E2B
tools.what: Hosted Firecracker sandboxes for agent code execution
tools.verdict: The hosted sandbox people build products on: per-session agent runs, untrusted code and preview environments. Volumes get praise; the cost is platform lock-in and limited customisation.

tools.name: nono
tools.what: Kernel-enforced Landlock/Seatbelt sandbox for coding agents
tools.verdict: Runs agents under Landlock or Seatbelt without a VM, so installed tooling still works, and can inject phantom credentials. Liked, but policy config is fiddlier than Anthropic's srt.

tools.name: smolvm
tools.what: Lightweight cross-platform microVMs for agent sandboxing
tools.verdict: Where users land after trying containers and OS sandboxes; praised as light and solid enough to build a whole agent harness on. Some fear a YC rug pull.

tools.name: yoloai
tools.what: Agent sandbox with copy-and-diff apply workflow
tools.verdict: Copies your workdir into a sandbox, hides API keys, and shows a diff before changes land. Most HN mentions come from its author; one tester calls the workflow not yet smooth.

tools.name: Lume
tools.what: macOS and Linux VM CLI for Apple Silicon
tools.verdict: A macOS and Linux VM manager on Apple's Virtualization framework, used to sandbox Claude or run macOS-only agents. Users call it reasonably good but report setup hoops and disk resizing glitches.

tools.name: Daytona
tools.what: Hosted sandbox infrastructure for AI agents
tools.verdict: Mostly named in lists of hosted agent sandboxes alongside E2B and Modal, and used as interchangeable infra in experiments. The one hands-on complaint: credits are near useless until higher usage tiers.

tools.name: Ardent
tools.what: Copy-on-write Postgres branches for agents
tools.verdict: Gives each agent run its own copy-on-write Postgres clone so a bad query cannot touch production. HN evidence is only the founder's own posts, so there is no independent user signal yet.

tools.name: container-use
tools.what: Dagger's containerised environments for coding agents
tools.verdict: Dagger's tool for giving each coding agent its own container environment. The one real HN comment objects that it requires docker group access by default.

tools.name: Ollama
tools.what: Local model runner with paid cloud tier
tools.verdict: The easy path to local Qwen and Gemma, and increasingly a paid cloud plan for hosted open models like DeepSeek Flash and GLM. Few complaints beyond local models feeling limited.

tools.name: llama.cpp
tools.what: C/C++ inference engine and llama-server
tools.verdict: A single fast binary that people move to from Ollama for control, usually serving models via llama-server. Complaints are about ROCm build friction and new flags that can cut speed.

tools.name: MLX
tools.what: Apple's array framework for Apple Silicon ML
tools.verdict: The Apple Silicon route to local inference, via MLX-Serve, LM Studio or custom engines. Praised for speed with less heat than a GPU box; some still prefer llama-server on Mac.

tools.name: LM Studio
tools.what: Desktop GUI app for running local models
tools.verdict: The GUI on-ramp for local models, often paired with Aider, Continue or Cline and praised for easy setup and model switching. Newer gripe: it now steers downloads to its agentic app.

tools.name: Open WebUI
tools.what: Self-hosted chat UI for local and API models
tools.verdict: The usual self-hosted chat front end over Ollama, llama.cpp or APIs, extended with plugins and Open Terminal. Feature-rich, but wiring up tools like search is painful and setup feels heavy.

tools.name: vLLM
tools.what: High-throughput GPU inference and serving engine
tools.verdict: The pick for batching and throughput on dedicated GPUs, run stock by self-hosters with multi-GPU rigs. Seen as harder to deploy than llama.cpp, with reports of engine bugs on long contexts.

tools.name: Unsloth
tools.what: Quantized model builds, fine-tuning and desktop app
tools.verdict: Best known as the source of quantized GGUFs people actually run, with even IQ1 DeepSeek quants holding up. Unsloth Desktop is gaining fans; complaints are tight context limits and no VRAM-to-RAM splitting.

tools.name: Lemonade
tools.what: AMD's local LLM server for GPU and NPU
tools.verdict: AMD's all-in-one local server and the go-to on Strix Halo, with easy installers and one endpoint for chat, images and speech. Owners say it replaced most cloud use; one reports weaker speeds.

tools.name: SGLang
tools.what: High-performance LLM serving framework for GPU clusters
tools.verdict: A datacenter serving engine named alongside vLLM for multi-GPU inference. Recent talk centres on a Cloudflare KV-cache leak involving an SGLang state bug, though some put the blame on Cloudflare's config.

tools.name: llama-swap
tools.what: Model-swapping proxy in front of llama-server
tools.verdict: The proxy home-lab users put in front of llama.cpp to hot-swap models behind one OpenAI-style endpoint. Called bulletproof by fans; critics say it adds hard-to-debug complexity now llama-server can juggle models itself.

tools.name: Apfel
tools.what: CLI and API for Apple's on-device model
tools.verdict: Wraps Apple's on-device Foundation Model as a CLI and OpenAI-style server, so the Mac's built-in model answers quick shell questions. Liked as useful; Apple's own first-party server may now overlap it.

tools.name: Jan
tools.what: Open-source desktop chat app for local models
tools.verdict: The open-source desktop alternative to LM Studio: a simple chat window that searches and downloads GGUF models with no lock-in. Often recommended as an easy start; the threads hold no real complaints.

tools.name: KoboldCpp
tools.what: Single-file llama.cpp runner with built-in UI
tools.verdict: One executable bundling llama.cpp with a web UI, image generation and speech, favoured by roleplay users for its tunables. Praised for zero-install simplicity, if a bit jack of all trades.

tools.name: OpenRouter
tools.what: Pay-as-you-go API router across model providers
tools.verdict: The pay-as-you-go side door to open-weight models like DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi, used to test models, run side projects and get past refusals. Main gripe: frontier models cost more there than subscriptions.

tools.name: AWS Bedrock
tools.what: AWS managed API for Claude and other models
tools.verdict: How companies buy Claude and other models at work: API pricing, budgets tracked with AWS spend, stronger privacy guarantees. Works well, but it costs more than Anthropic's own subscriptions.

tools.name: LiteLLM
tools.what: Python SDK and proxy unifying LLM APIs
tools.verdict: The common self-hosted gateway that teams point tools at for cheap multi-model access and token metering. Talk now centres on its PyPI supply-chain compromise and whether it can be trusted.

tools.name: OpenCode Go / Zen
tools.what: OpenCode's subscription and pay-per-use model access
tools.verdict: The budget pick: $10 a month buys generous open-weight usage, mostly DeepSeek Flash, and users rarely hit limits. The one knock is free Zen models rotating into the paid tier.

tools.name: Claude Code Router
tools.what: Proxy routing Claude Code to other models
tools.verdict: The usual way to keep Claude Code's harness while swapping in Kimi, Grok, DeepSeek or local Qwen, handy when quota runs out. One user found tool-call translation never fully lined up.

tools.name: llm (Simon Willison)
tools.what: CLI and Python library for many LLMs
tools.verdict: Simon Willison's CLI and Python library for prompting any model through plugins, with exportable logs. Others build plugins and IPython tools on it and praise its docs; core releases have slowed.

tools.name: Vercel AI Gateway
tools.what: Vercel's hosted multi-provider model API gateway
tools.verdict: Shows up mainly as where new models launch, sometimes free, and as a pay-per-token work account. Gripes: a required credit card, and third-party routing with the usual provider quality issues.

tools.name: cc-switch
tools.what: Provider switcher for Claude Code and Codex
tools.verdict: A switcher that points Claude Code or Codex at cheaper models like MiniMax or DeepSeek, translating between API formats. Thin evidence, but the users who mention it are happy.

tools.name: Portkey
tools.what: Hosted AI gateway with routing and logging
tools.verdict: An AI gateway that shows up in benchmark comparisons against LiteLLM and Bifrost. The one hands-on report switched from LiteLLM's proxy on the free plan and found it much faster.

tools.name: Chutes
tools.what: Decentralised GPU inference with TEE-served models
tools.verdict: Cheap open-model inference from trusted execution environments, so GPU owners cannot read prompts. One newcomer found no documented route into OpenCode or Claude Code.

tools.name: OmniRoute
tools.what: Self-hosted local router for model providers
tools.verdict: A self-hosted router for model APIs, named once as someone's local counterpart to OpenRouter. Too little HN discussion to judge it.

tools.name: Cloudflare AI Gateway
tools.what: Cloudflare proxy for LLM calls with spend controls
tools.verdict: A proxy in front of model APIs for monitoring, caching and spend caps without hosting your own. Complaints: budgets are fixed-window rules and reported prices can be wrong.

tools.name: Synthetic
tools.what: Subscription API for open-weight models
tools.verdict: A flat subscription for open-weight models such as DeepSeek Flash, pitched at OpenCode users. The only HN mention is from a cofounder, so there is no independent signal.

tools.name: LangChain
tools.what: Python and JS framework for LLM apps
tools.verdict: Still the default résumé keyword and a common base for internal RAG chatbots. Users say it works but adds overhead and latency, and some builders advertise skipping it entirely.

tools.name: Mastra
tools.what: Open-source TypeScript framework for AI agents
tools.verdict: The TypeScript agent framework with the warmest comments. A heavy user runs production agents on it, and a bug reporter says the CTO fixed eval scoring bugs within nine hours.

tools.name: Claude Agent SDK
tools.what: Anthropic's SDK exposing the Claude Code harness
tools.verdict: Most discussion is about billing: whether it can run on a Claude subscription, which the docs now confirm. Builders note it inherits Claude Code's heavy system prompts, and telemetry takes hacks.

tools.name: LangGraph
tools.what: Graph-based agent orchestration library from LangChain
tools.verdict: Mostly a résumé keyword next to LangChain. Where people describe it, they reach for it when they want deterministic, graph-shaped control over multi-step agent workflows.

tools.name: DSPy
tools.what: Stanford framework for programming and optimizing LLM prompts
tools.verdict: Loved by a vocal few for small classification and extraction tasks done in a few lines. Skeptics say plain agent loops beat DSPy-built agents in their own evals.

tools.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
tools.what: Microsoft's open-source .NET and Python agent framework
tools.verdict: Shows up mostly in .NET and Azure shops, in job posts and as the C# answer for MCP-based agents. Few hands-on reviews; one commenter notes its harness is still single-player.

tools.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
tools.what: OpenAI's lightweight Python multi-agent SDK
tools.verdict: Common in résumés and enterprise orchestrators. The one detailed user report praises it for wiring sandbox, Slack and knowledge-base integrations while controlling exactly what gets exposed to OpenAI.

tools.name: Google ADK
tools.what: Google's open-source Agent Development Kit
tools.verdict: Google's agent kit, used for sequential and looping multi-agent setups. It ships features fast enough to obsolete in-house work, but its LiteLLM dependency drew complaints after LiteLLM's vulnerability.

tools.name: CrewAI
tools.what: Python framework for role-based multi-agent crews
tools.verdict: An early multi-agent framework that now shows up mainly as a résumé keyword. The one experience report says agents left to coordinate themselves collaborate awkwardly unless the spec defines roles.

tools.name: Pydantic AI
tools.what: Type-safe Python agent framework from Pydantic
tools.verdict: A Python favourite among people leaving LangChain. Users like its provider abstractions on their own and use it as a thin base for small headless agents.

tools.name: MCP SDKs
tools.what: Official SDKs for building MCP servers and clients
tools.verdict: In practice this means FastMCP: a one-line import for wrapping APIs as MCP servers. Complaints are deployment gotchas like localhost-only DNS rebinding defaults, and doubts that MCP beats plain OpenAPI.

tools.name: Vercel AI SDK
tools.what: TypeScript toolkit for LLM apps and streaming
tools.verdict: The default TypeScript LLM toolkit in résumés and provider integrations, with its stream protocol ported as far as Ruby. Comments describe usage, not opinions.

tools.name: Strands Agents
tools.what: AWS's open-source model-driven agent SDK
tools.verdict: AWS's agent SDK, used with Bedrock for things like log-digging devops agents and a talking Raspberry Pi fish. One user hit a cache TTL issue; another questioned what Strands Harness adds.

tools.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI
tools.what: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for LLM telemetry
tools.verdict: The plumbing under most LLM observability tools rather than something people debate. People instrument API calls so agents can query a local collector, and export LLM traces to vendors like Braintrust.

tools.name: promptfoo
tools.what: Open-source CLI for prompt evals and red-teaming
tools.verdict: The go-to for personal regression evals: people use it to check prompts before switching models and to build benchmarks for their own workflow. Its team has since joined OpenAI.

tools.name: Langfuse
tools.what: Open-source LLM tracing, evals and prompt management
tools.verdict: The default open-source pick for LLM tracing, evals and prompt management, all over résumés. Users note a processing lag on traces, which a reply blames on outdated SDKs, and limited chart customisation.

tools.name: Arize Phoenix
tools.what: Open-source LLM tracing and eval platform
tools.verdict: Open-source tracing and eval tool people use for LLM-as-judge and production trace analysis. Evidence is thin, and one user found its Claude Code tracing setup heavy.

tools.name: MLflow
tools.what: Open-source ML lifecycle and experiment tracking platform
tools.verdict: The established ML experiment tracker, now also used for agent tracing. Those who tried MLflow 3's agent observability liked its session capture and metadata like files touched and model used.

tools.name: Logfire
tools.what: Pydantic's OpenTelemetry-based observability platform
tools.verdict: Pydantic's tracing service, often paired with Pydantic AI. Users call it very helpful for diagnosing agent bugs; one who tried both found it similar to Langfuse but with fewer eval features.

tools.name: Opik
tools.what: Comet's open-source LLM tracing and eval tool
tools.verdict: Comet's open-source LLM tracing and eval tool, with little discussion. Mentions call it useful for LLMOps, and one contributor fixed streaming wrappers that were swallowing exceptions.

tools.name: Braintrust
tools.what: Hosted LLM eval and observability platform
tools.verdict: A hosted eval platform that shows up in startup stacks like Curai's. The few opinions call it solid for evals; its top HN story is a confirmed breach.

tools.name: Helicone
tools.what: Open-source LLM gateway and observability proxy
tools.verdict: Known as much for its LLM cost page as its gateway. Self-hosters found almost no setup docs, cost analysis needs your own SQL, and the service is now in maintenance mode.

tools.name: DeepEval
tools.what: Open-source Python framework for LLM evals
tools.verdict: A Python eval library used mostly for RAG checks and LLM-as-judge assertions. Advice threads pitch it as the code-first option next to promptfoo's YAML.

tools.name: LangSmith
tools.what: LangChain's hosted tracing and eval service
tools.verdict: LangChain's tracing and eval service, mostly a résumé line next to LangGraph, sometimes the eval harness for production agent systems. The one hands-on report dropped it for adding latency.

tools.name: Inspect AI
tools.what: UK AISI's open-source LLM evaluation framework
tools.verdict: The UK AI Security Institute's eval framework. HN barely discusses it: one résumé, one PR link, and someone planning to try it alongside promptfoo.

tools.name: garak
tools.what: NVIDIA's open-source LLM vulnerability scanner
tools.verdict: NVIDIA's LLM vulnerability scanner. It appears only in red-teaming tool lists next to PyRIT; most HN hits for the name are about the Star Trek character.

tools.name: OpenClaw
tools.what: Open-source always-on personal AI agent
tools.verdict: The personal agent many tried and most have retired. A few keep it for event-driven chores and calendar nudges; the rest cite constant tinkering, crashes after a week and poor local-model support.

tools.name: Hermes Agent
tools.what: Nous Research's open-source persistent personal agent
tools.verdict: The personal agent with the most loyal users, run on Mac Minis or VPSes, reached via Telegram, often on local models. Detractors cite a dated UI and regressions between updates.

tools.name: Muse
tools.what: Meta's consumer personal AI agent
tools.verdict: Meta's consumer agent. Fans use it for research, forum scraping and group marketing, but most comments cite privacy incidents, ignored permissions, a 0-day, and slowness.

tools.name: Claude Cowork
tools.what: Claude's desktop agent for non-coding work
tools.verdict: Claude's agent for non-coding work, used for email, todos, receipts and business operations, including by non-developers. One complaint: it floods teams with AI slop that reviewers must clean up.

tools.name: n8n
tools.what: Fair-code visual workflow automation platform
tools.verdict: The workflow automation tool AI and automation freelancers list on résumés, used for chores like filing tax records and forwarding email. One comment calls its open-core licensing direction a mess.

tools.name: NanoClaw
tools.what: Minimal container-isolated OpenClaw alternative in TypeScript
tools.verdict: A lightweight, container-isolated OpenClaw alternative some find easier to understand. Several users moved on to Hermes or hand-rolled agents, and one ditched it as useless for email triage.

tools.name: Home Assistant + LLM
tools.what: Home Assistant's LLM conversation and voice integrations
tools.verdict: Home Assistant's LLM and voice hooks, often run on local models. People wire it to MCP servers for voice control and EV charging plans, though LLMs can struggle with the unofficial MCP.

tools.name: Claude Duet
tools.what: Anthropic's proactive agent for professionals, in preview
tools.verdict: Anthropic's waitlisted proactive agent, still in research preview. Early users run it for monitoring communications, but find it slow and say OpenAI's Dots is better today.

tools.name: Dots
tools.what: OpenAI's persistent personal agent
tools.verdict: OpenAI's persistent personal agent. One user built a speculative Lean-verified proof with a Dots swarm, another rates it above Duet; critics dislike the cutesy branding and a confusing product lineup.

tools.name: Paperclip
tools.what: Open-source org chart for running agent companies
tools.verdict: An open-source tool for running a 'company' of agents with an org chart. HN mentions are passing comparisons, with no hands-on reports.

tools.name: Claude Code Routines
tools.what: Scheduled, cloud-run Claude Code agent jobs
tools.verdict: Scheduled Claude Code jobs, essentially agent cron. People see it as a cheaper subscription path for PR review bots, but several say a local cron job does the same.

tools.name: nanobot
tools.what: Ultra-lightweight open-source OpenClaw alternative
tools.verdict: An ultra-lightweight open-source alternative to OpenClaw from HKUDS. None of the matched HN comments discuss it; every hit is about sci-fi nanobots.

tools.name: Eigent
tools.what: Open-source desktop alternative to Claude Cowork
tools.verdict: An open-source desktop alternative to Claude Cowork. HN evidence is effectively nil: one bare link, with every other match being German 'eigentlich' or EigenTrust.
